Sorry, but it is impossible to meet this forecast target with some reasonable probability by any of the given deadlines.

Each so-called "Millenium prize problem" has been open for at least a few decades. They are extremely difficult, wth no known approaches to start to think of solving them. Indeed, most experts in every field believe that a solution needs radical new ideas and insights to be found, that would only come from a prodigiously talented genius mathematician - and that implies that this should not be expected over the next 5 years, let alone 150 years.

What are the chances that over the next 5 years, one of the most intelligent systems ever built by humankind (that somehow remained mostly unable to read and write or try other forms of communication with the outside, let alone reaching its ultimate capabilities) would happen to identify sequences of symbols that could qualify as a solution to some of these classic open problems in less than 20 years of incremental progress since their actual statement?

It is likely that AI may someday be able to help with some proofs - by proving some intermediate statements, or helping to check things, or similar applications. But it's also likely that its greatest achievement, over decades of development, may have a hard time being that hard. Its only competition is the brightest young people, of whom I suspect that there should be many that could already solve all these (or find better solutions to them than those given in 2000 by Clay).

AI, although achieving amazing feats, is extremely far from having the level of mental (neural) hardware of a human being. I suspect that its greatest achievements could likely come from its advanced capabilities in finding patterns and connections. That said, even the best AIs from 50 years ago would have been the only ones to find them back then, had their hardware been immediately declined to the level of our current computer hardware (requiring an investment in improving the design it had into modern technology).

In that sense, I think that an expert AI built with modern computer hardware should have the opportunity of "stage leveling" it away from the rest - along with other advances in turning it from a single, redundant processor, to a more distributed version at a level closer to our brain. I expect mastery of languages may even depend on that - although spoken and visual languages may be solved by a single AI containing everything needed to even read and understand modern papers.

Unfortunately, in such a scenario whose evolution of intelligence cannot be predicted and expanded, I even doubt that clued P=NP would be solved by such an expert system.

Of course, an important element to consider is time limits: if the timelines to develop such an expert system remains should realistically remain less than a few years, then it could stand its chance. However, vast experimentation has already shown that this should require time limits that would be near hopeless to meet, within the 5 or 10 years currently known. Larger alisences would have vastly larger hardware, potentially superhuman according to various metrics.

A more reasonable target for such an ambitious system could be tens of thousands of years, which would allow for all the evolution of computer hardware to come down in price over time. In that future, we may also find a very hard way where human researcher wouldn't even better the best AI even through . Nevertheless, agreed that a 10,000 year-times timeline is very unlikely in the timeline of humanity.

To summarize, the expected difficulty may be that an expert AI able to solve one of these problems in a time frame of benefit would still need a talent level amongst the world's best mathemeticians, since surely the world's best competing diretly involved in these open problems - presumably tens of mill^-window when any "expert AI" system would be able to compete to any more engaged talent of a weaker absolute level, only becoming able to compete with the top few really talented mathematicians.

In all, the probability of reaching any actual solution within any of these deadlines, despite AI's time for progress being near linear, is highly improbable, as is having it having solver a problem still requiring significant further progress.

formatted_prompt:
<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
